name: Polynucleotide eye filler

card.summary: Polynucleotide injections around the eyes for thin, crepey lower-lid skin; very little published evidence turned up for the periorbital use.
card.aka: Periorbital polynucleotide injections, PN eye treatment
card.note: Thin source base; no clinical studies of the eye-area use were found.

quick.overview:
Polynucleotide eye filler refers to injections of polynucleotide-based products into the thin skin around the eyes. The intent is to improve skin quality in the periorbital area rather than to add large volume.

Very little documentation was found for this use. A registered observational study of a periorbital rejuvenation procedure (n=29) exists, but its listing does not specify the product, so no studies were found for polynucleotide eye treatment specifically.
quick.mechanism: Proponents of polynucleotide injectables describe them as stimulating skin repair and hydration. No published eyelid-specific mechanism data were found in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Injections near the eye carry the general risks of periorbital injectables, including bruising, swelling and lumpiness, and the thin skin shows irregularities. No specific safety data for this use were found in the sources reviewed.

lead: Polynucleotide eye filler is the name for injections of polynucleotide-based products into the thin skin of the lower eyelid and surrounding area. The aim is a smoother, fresher-looking under-eye area, with skin that looks less thin, crepey or tired, rather than added volume.

Polynucleotides are chains of nucleotides such as DNA and RNA, and Wikipedia notes that fish-derived polynucleotide is used in aesthetic medicine as a skin injectable [1]. Practitioners and proponents describe the products as skin-quality treatments that support repair and hydration, and the eye area is one of the sites where they are offered.

Published evidence on the periorbital use is sparse. A registered prospective, non-interventional study of a periorbital rejuvenation procedure (n=29, completed 2025) lists glabellar lines, midface volume deficiency and periorbital wrinkling as conditions, but the listing does not identify the product used [2].

paras: Polynucleotide products are used in aesthetic medicine as skin injectables, and fish-derived polynucleotide is the type described in Wikipedia's entry [1]. Eye-area treatment targets the delicate skin of the lower lid, where irregularities are easy to see. Provider-specific protocols and product names vary and are not documented in independent sources.

Injections near the eye carry the general risks of periorbital injectables, including bruising, swelling and lumpiness, and the thin skin shows irregularities. No safety data specific to polynucleotides at this site were found.
No studies found. A registered non-interventional study assessing a periorbital rejuvenation procedure enrolled 29 participants, but the registration does not name polynucleotides [2].

angle.text: People seek the treatment for thin, crepey or tired-looking skin under the eyes. Proponents describe the injectables as improving skin quality in that area; eyelid-specific data have not been published [1][2].
